nameStory: Tree pelt lichen gets its name from its animal hide-like appearance - the thallus (lichen body) looks remarkably like a small furry pelt spread across tree bark. The word 'pelt' comes from the Latin 'pellis' meaning skin, which perfectly captures how this lichen drapes and contours to its host tree like a flexible animal hide.
description: Tree pelt lichen is a leafy, foliose lichen that forms grayish-green to brownish patches on tree bark, typically 2-6 inches across. Like all lichens, it's actually two organisms living together - a fungus and an alga working as a team to survive. The upper surface has a soft, velvety texture when dry, while the underside is pale with dark veins and root-like structures called rhizines that anchor it to the bark. This species is quite rare in New England, making any sighting special.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms large, leafy lobes that lie flat against tree bark like overlapping pieces of leather, with edges that curl up slightly when dry

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface feels soft and slightly fuzzy when dry, almost like velvet or suede, becoming smoother and more pliable when wet

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green to olive-brown when moist, turning more grayish or brownish when dry, with the color change being quite noticeable

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always found growing on tree bark, particularly favoring hardwood trees like maples and oaks rather than conifers

idTips.label: Underside
idTips.description: Pale whitish to cream colored underneath with dark brown to black branching veins and scattered dark rhizines that feel slightly rough

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual thalli typically 2-6 inches across, sometimes growing larger on favorable trees, with lobes about 0.5-1 inch wide

habitat: Tree pelt lichen grows on the bark of deciduous trees in mature forests, particularly favoring maples, oaks, and other hardwoods in areas with good air quality. Look for it in established woodlands with high humidity, often in valleys or protected areas where moisture lingers. It prefers locations with some shelter from direct sunlight but still receives filtered light.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant after spring rains when the thallus is fully hydrated and shows its greenish colors most clearly. This is an excellent time to observe the texture differences between wet and dry states.
seasonality.summer: May appear duller and more contracted during dry spells, with edges curling up noticeably. Early morning dew can temporarily restore the fresh appearance.
seasonality.fall: Often looks its best in the humid conditions of autumn, with colors appearing richer against the backdrop of falling leaves. The contrast with colorful fall foliage makes it easier to spot.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible but may be partially obscured by snow. Ice and freezing rain can make the lichen appear darker and more compressed against the bark.

funFact: Tree pelt lichen is so rare in New England that it has only been officially documented once in the region - making anyone who spots it a true lichen detective contributing to scientific knowledge about its distribution!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the more common dog pelt lichen, but tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety texture when dry and tends to be more brownish rather than grayish-green. Remember: 'tree pelt feels like velvet, dog pelt feels more papery.'
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'collina' means 'of the hills,' though this doesn't necessarily mean you'll only find it on hillsides - early botanists who named it may have first collected it in hilly terrain. Like many rare lichens, tree pelt lichen is sensitive to air pollution, so its presence indicates good environmental quality.
compareHints: Compared to its Peltigera relatives, tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety surface texture and tends to be more brownish in color than the grayer dog pelt lichen or the more distinctly veined fan pelt lichen. Its lobes are also typically broader and more rounded than the narrow, finger-like projections of many-fruited pelt lichen. The combination of the soft texture and brownish color helps distinguish it from other pelt lichens in the area.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
Among the many pelt lichens in New England, field dog lichen stands out for its incredibly soft, velvety surface texture - most other dog lichens feel smoother or more leathery.
Carpet pelt lichen differs from its pelt lichen relatives by its consistently smooth upper surface and preference for soil rather than rocks or trees.

Among the many pelt lichen species in New England, membranous pelt lichen stands out for its distinctly thin, papery texture - much more delicate than the thicker, more leathery dog pelt lichen or scaly pelt lichen.
Unlike the smooth-surfaced dog pelt lichen or the powdery-edged freckled pelt lichen, mother-of-many pelt is immediately recognizable by its bumpy, phyllidia-covered surface.

Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has rounded, disk-like apothecia along the lobe edges, blacksaddle pelt has distinctive tubular, saddle-shaped reproductive structures on the lichen surface.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, fan pelt lichen stands out with its smooth upper surface and distinctive raised black veins underneath.

Among pelt lichens, the pale-bellied pelt is distinguished by its consistently pale underside, whereas dog pelt lichen has a darker, often brownish underside with prominent veins, and freckled pelt lichen has distinctive dark spots on its upper surface.
